[3, 4, 5] The laureates' work with these tiny nanoparticles, whose properties are determined by their size, is significant for nanotechnology. Ekimov is credited with discovering the size-dependent quantum effects in nanoparticles in the early 1980s while working at the Vavilov State Optical Institute, laying the groundwork for the field. Prediction target period: from 2024-10-27 to 2025-01-12. Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> The University of Chicago held a news conference on October 14, 2024, to celebrate Professor James A. Robinson, who was awarded the 2024 Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel. [2, 8, 10] Robinson, a University Professor at the Harris School of Public Policy, shared the prize with Daron Acemoglu and Simon Johnson of MIT for their research on how institutions form and affect prosperity. [3, 5, 7] The press conference featured remarks from University of Chicago President Paul Alivisatos and Ethan Bueno de Mesquita, the dean of the Harris School of Public Policy. [2, 10] <2> The 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry was awarded to three scientists for their revolutionary work on proteins. One half of the prize was awarded to American scientist David Baker for "computational protein design." The other half was jointly awarded to Demis Hassabis of the United Kingdom and John M. Jumper of the United States, both of Google DeepMind, for their work on "protein structure prediction." Baker's research enabled the creation of entirely new proteins with novel functions, while Hassabis and Jumper developed an AI model, AlphaFold2, that can accurately predict the complex three-dimensional structures of proteins from their amino acid sequences. This work has solved a 50-year-old challenge in biology and has transformative potential for medicine, pharmaceuticals, and nanotechnology. <3> American scientist John J. Hopfield, from Princeton University, and Geoffrey E. Hinton of the University of Toronto were jointly awarded the 2024 Nobel Prize in Physics. The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences recognized them "for foundational discoveries and inventions that enable machine learning with artificial neural networks". Their work, which dates back to the 1980s, applied concepts from physics to develop artificial neural networks. Hopfield created an associative memory network capable of storing and retrieving patterns, while Hinton developed learning algorithms, such as the Boltzmann machine, that allow networks to find properties in data autonomously. These discoveries are fundamental to modern artificial intelligence and are used in a wide array of applications, including facial recognition, language translation, and developing new materials. The prize money of 11 million Swedish kronor is to be shared equally between the laureates. <4> On October 7, 2024, the Nobel Assembly at Karolinska Institutet announced that Americans Victor Ambros and Gary Ruvkun were jointly awarded the 2024 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. [2, 4, 6] The prize recognizes their discovery of microRNA (miRNA) and its role in post-transcriptional gene regulation. [3, 5] Their work, which began with studies of the nematode C. elegans in 1993, uncovered a new and previously unknown mechanism for controlling gene expression. [10] They found that these small RNA molecules can regulate gene activity by binding to messenger RNA (mRNA), which prevents it from being translated into a protein. [2] This discovery has revealed a new dimension of gene regulation that is crucial for the development and function of cells in multicellular organisms, including humans. [7, 10] The dysregulation of microRNA has been linked to various diseases, and their findings have significant implications for research into cancer, cardiovascular disease, and other genetic and metabolic conditions. [1, 8, 10] Clinical trials are now underway for microRNA-based therapeutics. [7] <5> On September 19, 2024, Clarivate announced its 2024 Citation Laureates, identifying 22 researchers whose work is considered to be of Nobel class due to its significant impact and high citation rates. Among those named for their work in protein structures were American scientist David Baker of the University of Washington, along with John M. Jumper and Demis Hassabis of Google DeepMind. The predictions were validated weeks later when the 2024 Nobel Prizes were announced. On October 7, 2024, the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine was jointly awarded to Victor Ambros and Gary Ruvkun for their discovery of microRNA and its role in gene regulation; Clarivate had previously named them Citation Laureates in 2008. On October 9, 2024, David Baker, John M. Jumper, and Demis Hassabis were awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry. The prize recognized Baker for "computational protein design" and Jumper and Hassabis jointly for "protein structure prediction." <6> In a recurring poll by ChemistryViews magazine, readers predicted that an American biochemist was the most likely winner of the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. According to the poll results published on September 13, 2024, the most frequently suggested potential laureates were American biochemist Chi-Huey Wong, known for his work in glycoscience, American-Jordanian chemist Omar M. Yaghi, a pioneer in developing metal-organic frameworks (MOFs), and Shankar Balasubramanian from the University of Cambridge for his contributions to next-generation sequencing. [4, 5, 6, 7] Subsequent updates to the poll in October showed shifts in the top predictions, though Wong and Yaghi remained prominent candidates. [1, 2] Ultimately, the Nobel Prize in Chemistry 2024 was awarded on October 9, 2024, to David Baker for computational protein design, and jointly to Demis Hassabis and John Jumper for protein structure prediction, a different set of laureates than those favored in the September poll. [12] <7> Nobel laureate Michael Levitt, a professor of structural biology at Stanford University, was awarded the 2024 Rev. Joseph Carrier, C.S.C. Science Medal by the University of Notre Dame's College of Science on September 9, 2024. The medal, the most prestigious awarded by the college, honored Levitt for his significant achievements in science, particularly his foundational work in developing computer models of chemical reactions. The award ceremony took place in the Dahnke Ballroom at Notre Dame Stadium. As part of the event, Levitt delivered a lecture titled, “Multidisciplinary Revolution in Biology and Artificial Intelligence,” which was followed by a fireside chat and a reception. The lecture and ceremony are archived and available to view online. <8> Daniel Kahneman, an Israeli-American psychologist and Nobel laureate, passed away on March 27, 2024, at the age of 90. His death was confirmed by his stepdaughter, Deborah Treisman. Kahneman, a professor of psychology and public affairs emeritus at Princeton University, was awarded the 2002 Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences for his influential work on the psychology of judgment and decision-making, which laid the foundation for behavioral economics. His research, often conducted with his late collaborator Amos Tversky, challenged the traditional economic assumption of rational human behavior by demonstrating the cognitive biases and mental shortcuts that affect decision-making. This work was famously detailed in his best-selling book, "Thinking, Fast and Slow". At the time of his Nobel win, Kahneman was a professor at Princeton University, having joined the faculty in 1993. In 2013, he was awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom by President Barack Obama. <9> The 60th annual Nobel Conference, the only event in the United States authorized to use the Nobel name by the Nobel Foundation, was held at Gustavus Adolphus College in St. Peter, Minnesota, on October 1-2, 2024. The theme for the 2024 conference was “Sleep, Unraveled.” The event brought together an interdisciplinary panel of experts in fields such as neuroscience, biochemistry, and psychiatry to explore the science, culture, and social implications of sleep. Topics included the neurological processes of sleep, the evolution of sleep practices, teen sleep, circadian health, and the societal consequences of sleep deprivation. For the first time, the event was free and open to the public, with options to attend in person at the college's Christ Chapel or view via a live stream. The conference featured seven keynote speakers and panel discussions, complemented by art exhibitions and other cultural events related to the theme. <10> Claudia Goldin of Harvard University was awarded the Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel 2023 for her extensive research that has advanced the understanding of women's outcomes in the labor market. [2, 6, 8] The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences announced the award on October 9, 2023, recognizing Goldin for providing the first comprehensive account of women's earnings and labor market participation over the centuries, highlighting the causes of change and the primary sources of the continuing gender gap. [2, 3] Goldin is the third woman to receive the economics prize. [6, 8] The official award ceremony took place in Stockholm, Sweden, on December 10, 2023, the anniversary of Alfred Nobel's death. [1, 7]

In a significant moment during the conference, participants acknowledged the 2024 Nobel Peace Prize awarded to Nihon Hidankyo, the Japanese confederation of A- and H-bomb sufferers' organizations, for their extensive efforts toward a world free of nuclear weapons and their testimony on the catastrophic consequences of their use. The treaty itself is a product of the efforts of the 2017 Nobel Peace Prize laureate, the International Campaign to Abolish Nuclear Weapons (ICAN). The meeting's political declaration firmly rejected nuclear weapons and challenged the concept of nuclear deterrence. <4> The University of Washington's School of Pharmacy held its 2025 Nudelman Lecture, titled “The AI Frontier,” on March 6, 2025. The event featured a lecture by Dr. David Baker, a professor of biochemistry at the University of Washington School of Medicine and director of the UW Medicine Institute for Protein Design. Dr. Baker was awarded the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for his work on computational protein design, sharing the prize with Demis Hassabis and John M. Jumper of Google DeepMind. He is also a member of the executive committee for the university's WE-REACH leadership team. The announcement for the lecture was published on March 4, 2025. <5> On March 5, 2025, which was also Ash Wednesday, a coalition of anti-nuclear groups including the Atlantic Life Community, War Resisters League, Nukewatch, and Veterans For Peace, held a protest at the U.S. Mission to the United Nations in New York City. Protesters urged the United States to join the TPNW, a treaty created through the efforts of the 2017 Nobel Peace Prize laureate, the International Campaign to Abolish Nuclear Weapons (ICAN). Activists blocked First Avenue with banners, one of which read “U.S. Join the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons,” and wheatpasted the text of the treaty in front of the U.S. Mission. Robinson, who was awarded the 2024 Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel. [2, 8, 10] Robinson, a University Professor at the Harris School of Public Policy, shared the prize with Daron Acemoglu and Simon Johnson of MIT for their research on how institutions form and affect prosperity. Robinson. Their research was recognized "for studies of how institutions are formed and affect prosperity". One half of the prize was awarded to American scientist David Baker for "computational protein design." The other half was jointly awarded to Demis Hassabis of the United Kingdom and John M. Jumper of the United States, both of Google DeepMind, for their work on "protein structure prediction." Baker's research enabled the creation of entirely new proteins with novel functions, while Hassabis and Jumper developed an AI model, AlphaFold2, that can accurately predict the complex three-dimensional structures of proteins from their amino acid sequences. This work has solved a 50-year-old challenge in biology and has transformative potential for medicine, pharmaceuticals, and nanotechnology. <9> American scientist John J. Hopfield, from Princeton University, and Geoffrey E. Hinton of the University of Toronto were jointly awarded the 2024 Nobel Prize in Physics. The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences recognized them "for foundational discoveries and inventions that enable machine learning with artificial neural networks". Their work, which dates back to the 1980s, applied concepts from physics to develop artificial neural networks. Hopfield created an associative memory network capable of storing and retrieving patterns, while Hinton developed learning algorithms, such as the Boltzmann machine, that allow networks to find properties in data autonomously. These discoveries are fundamental to modern artificial intelligence and are used in a wide array of applications, including facial recognition, language translation, and developing new materials. The prize money of 11 million Swedish kronor is to be shared equally between the laureates.
